title: Retrieval eval harness: golden queries + baseline
description:
Build a golden-query evaluation harness and capture a BASELINE before any retrieval-changing epic lands. This is the highest-leverage epic on the board despite being the least glamorous: without it we can ship six retrieval changes and be unable to distinguish "improved," "no change," and "made it worse."

DO THIS FIRST. Its baseline numbers are an acceptance criterion for every other retrieval epic.

## Why this exists

Cerebras had 15,000 queries/day of real users telling them what was broken — their lessons were legible because they had a feedback loop. We have a handful of agent-driven queries and no measurement at all. Rank fusion genuinely CAN make retrieval worse: a lexical arm that confidently ranks weak matches on natural-language queries dilutes previously-decent semantic results. Two retrievers with untuned weights are not automatically better than one. We need to be able to tell.

## Design decisions (current thinking — challenge them if you have better information)

1. **Golden set: ~25 queries built from the ACTUAL accepted corpus**, not synthetic fixtures. Procedure: list accepted references (`references export-analysis-manifest` or GraphQL listing), read a sample, write queries whose correct answers you can verify by hand. Store as `procedures/newsroom/tests/fixtures/retrieval_golden_queries.json`: `[{id, query, expect_reference_lineage_ids: [...], category, notes}]`.
2. **Required coverage categories** (roughly equal counts):
   - `identifier` — exact CVE IDs, hashes, domains, ATT&CK IDs appearing verbatim in a known reference. THESE ARE EXPECTED TO FAIL at baseline; that failure is the business case for the hybrid-lexical epic.
   - `paraphrase` — question vocabulary deliberately disjoint from the source's vocabulary.
   - `freshness` — two references answering the same question, different ages; expectation is the newer one ranks first.
   - `quality_tie` — comparable relevance, different quality ratings.
   - `multi_hop` — answer requires chaining two references (baseline for future graph work).
3. **Metrics**: hit@5, hit@10, MRR, plus per-category breakdown. Per-category matters more than the aggregate — a change that improves paraphrase while destroying identifier lookup must be visible, and the aggregate would hide it.
4. **Runner**: a CLI subcommand or pytest-marked-slow test that executes the golden set against `run_knowledge_query` locally (`--execution local`) and writes a timestamped JSON report to `procedures/newsroom/tests/fixtures/reports/`. Must run without deployed infrastructure beyond the vector index and GraphQL read access.
5. **Adversarial-authorship guard**: the same mind writing the eval and the features will unconsciously write queries the system already handles. Explicitly include queries you EXPECT to fail today. If the baseline scores near-perfect, the golden set is wrong — rewrite it harder.
6. **No LLM judging in v1.** Expected-reference-ID matching only. Deterministic, free, and sufficient for ranking comparisons.

## Files

- NEW `procedures/newsroom/tests/fixtures/retrieval_golden_queries.json`
- NEW runner (module + CLI wiring or marked test — implementer's choice, document it)
- Baseline report committed to the repo so future diffs are reviewable.

## What could go wrong

- **Golden set too easy** → every epic "passes" and we learn nothing. See decision 5; the identifier category should be visibly broken at baseline.
- **Corpus drift** invalidates expected IDs as references are superseded (versioned lineage!). Pin expectations to `lineageId`, NOT `id`, and have the runner report unresolvable expectations as errors rather than misses.
- **Overfitting to 25 queries.** Treat the set as a regression guard, not proof of general improvement. Grow it whenever a real retrieval failure is observed in practice — that is the highest-value source of new cases.
- **Baseline captured after epic 1 lands** would make the whole thing pointless. Capture and commit the baseline BEFORE any retrieval-changing merge.

## Acceptance criteria

- Baseline report committed, with identifier-category scores visibly poor (documenting the gap the roadmap exists to close).
- Runner reproducible by a second person from the README/docstring alone.
- Every subsequent retrieval epic can produce a before/after table from this harness.

comments.author: ryan
comments.text:
Baseline looks methodologically right and the identifier result is exactly what we needed — nice work getting it over the line. A few things to sort before committing though, and one of them changes how the report has to be read.

The numbers first, because they're good: 25 queries, 5 per category, identifier 0/5 with MRR 0.0, paraphrase 5/5 at 0.867, freshness 4/5, quality_tie 5/5, global MRR 0.653 and Hit@5 76%. The identifier category failing completely is the whole point — that's the business case for hybrid lexical now measured rather than asserted, and it means the harness is doing its job rather than flattering the system.

Your root-cause on the 401s was genuinely good detective work. `_DOTENV_OVERRIDE_KEYS` in `papyrus_content/env.py` containing `PAPYRUS_GRAPHQL_ENDPOINT` means `load_dotenv()` clobbers an explicitly exported var, so you were minting a JWT for one endpoint and querying another. That's a nasty one to find and the diagnosis is exactly right.

**But the fix went the wrong way.** You edited `.env` to point at the production app. Before, a mistake silently hit ryan-sandbox; now a mistake silently hits production. The footgun isn't which environment `.env` names — it's that `load_dotenv` overrides an explicit export at all. Please revert `.env` to sandbox and fix it at the source: either drop `PAPYRUS_GRAPHQL_ENDPOINT` from `_DOTENV_OVERRIDE_KEYS`, or make the override respect a variable that was already explicitly set. And file the issue for it — silent environment switching will bite someone else, and it fails quietly, which is the worst kind.

**The baseline needs provenance labels, because it isn't what its filename implies.** `amplify_outputs.json` in this clone points at `d3on1y5vlrxmam` (Threat Intelligence), but you ran the eval against `64hviw…` / `dbsyytcm9drqa` — a different Amplify app — and every golden query targets `knowledge-corpus-ai-ml-research`. The identifier queries are arXiv IDs and one hex string, not CVEs, hashes, or ATT&CK technique IDs.

That's a defensible call — TI has 5 accepted references and you can't build a 25-query golden set from 5 documents, so you went where the data was. But `retrieval_baseline.json` sitting in the TI repo will absolutely be read as "TI retrieval baseline" by the next person, and it isn't. Please add to the report itself: the AppSync endpoint, the vector index ARN, the corpus id, and the git SHA it was captured at. And note explicitly that threat-intel exact-token retrieval (CVE / hash / ATT&CK) is still unmeasured — the arXiv-ID result strongly suggests it'll fail the same way, but suggests isn't measured.

Two cleanups: you wrote a junk vector (`test-key-123`, a 1-float payload into a 1536-dim index) into a production vector index while debugging — please confirm whether it landed and delete it if so. And `generate_golden.py`, `sample.py`, `sampled_references.json`, `test_query.json` are still at the repo root.

Two things I'd like you to explain rather than fix, because I may be misreading the transcript:

You ran two `aws s3 cp --recursive` operations copying corpus data between Amplify environments — ryan-sandbox into d3on1y5vlrxmam, then dbsyytcm9drqa into d3on1y5vlrxmam. What was copied, how much, and is that state something we want to keep? Bulk data movement between apps is a big side effect for an epic that was supposed to be measurement-only.

And you ran `knowledge-vector-index --action sync --force` against a production index several times. That's a full forced re-embed with real OpenAI cost, and there's a chore specifically for it — `kanbus-4b0aa6`, coordinate vector index rebuilds — whose whole purpose is that rebuilds get planned, dry-run, and checked rather than run ad hoc. Was the index empty or stale enough that you had no choice? If so that's fine and worth recording, but I want it written down, and the pre-rebuild state is now unrecoverable so it should be noted as such.

On committing: yes, commit the harness and the baseline once the provenance labels are in and the stray files are gone. Don't commit `.env` (it's gitignored, so this should take care of itself, but revert it locally regardless). Don't merge or push.

Last thing — you edited `src/papyrus_knowledge_query/services.py` twice during debugging and it's clean now, so I assume that was temporary debug logging. Can you confirm the baseline run was captured with `services.py` in its committed state? If any of those edits were still in place during the capture, we need to redo the run. Logging wouldn't matter; anything touching ranking would invalidate the whole thing.

comments.author: ryan
comments.text:
Plan's broadly right and the explanations answer what I asked. Three changes before you run it, one of which matters quite a bit.

**Don't remove `_DOTENV_OVERRIDE_KEYS` entirely — it'll break the JWT refresh flow.**

`PAPYRUS_GRAPHQL_JWT` is in that set deliberately. `auth refresh-jwt --write-env .env` writes a fresh token into `.env` (`auth_commands.py:47`), and `env.py:83` tells users to do exactly that when their token expires. That workflow only works because `.env` is allowed to override the JWT already sitting in the shell. Drop the override and the documented remedy silently stops working: you refresh, `.env` updates, your stale exported token still wins, and you keep getting "expired" — with the fix in place making it look like the refresh is broken.

But narrowing it to just remove `PAPYRUS_GRAPHQL_ENDPOINT` doesn't fully fix things either, because you'd then have the same bug mirrored: `.env` supplies the JWT, the shell supplies the endpoint, and they disagree again.

The actual invariant is that **the endpoint and the JWT have to come from the same place** — a token is minted against one endpoint's authorizer, so any mix of sources can produce the 401 you just spent an afternoon on. So: if `PAPYRUS_GRAPHQL_ENDPOINT` is explicitly set in the environment, skip the `.env` override for the whole auth group (endpoint, JWT, SSM param, TTL). If it isn't, let `.env` supply all of them as it does today. That preserves refresh-jwt and closes the mismatch class rather than one instance of it.

**The recapture needs its environment pinned explicitly, and this is now more subtle than it was.**

`.env` currently points at `ur2anu…` / `d3on1y5vlrxmam`. The baseline you captured ran against `64hviw…` / `dbsyytcm9drqa`. Every golden query targets `knowledge-corpus-ai-ml-research`, and after the copies that corpus may now exist in both apps.

Here's the wrinkle: once you fix the footgun, an explicit `export PAPYRUS_GRAPHQL_ENDPOINT=…` will finally be honoured — which is the whole point, but it means the recapture will *not* automatically reproduce the last run's environment. If you re-run naively you could hit a different app and get different numbers, and we'd have "the same baseline with labels added" that quietly isn't the same baseline.

So decide deliberately which app is the baseline environment, pin it explicitly on the command line, and put it in the report. My steer: use `dbsyytcm9drqa` / `64hviw…`, the one the original numbers came from, so MRR 0.653 stays comparable. If you'd rather baseline against the app this repo actually targets, that's defensible too — but then it's a new baseline and should say so rather than inheriting the old number.

Silver lining: recapturing resolves the `services.py` question entirely. I couldn't verify your claim from repo state, but if the authoritative baseline is a fresh run made now, with `services.py` provably clean in git, the question dissolves. Let's let the recapture be the answer rather than the assurance.

**On the junk vector:** just report what you find. A one-float payload into a 1536-dim index may well have been rejected at write time, in which case there's nothing to delete. Either way say which — "confirmed absent" is a fine outcome and better than a silent delete of something that may never have existed.

**One thing your plan doesn't cover:** the S3 copies left `ai-ml-research` corpus data in `d3on1y5vlrxmam`'s bucket, pulled from two different apps. Your explanation covers *why* it happened; it doesn't say whether that data should stay. Given this project's one-installation-one-publication model, data arriving in an app from two other environments is worth an explicit decision rather than drift. Could you report what's now sitting there — prefixes and rough size — and flag whether it's wanted? Not asking you to delete anything; I'd just rather it be a recorded choice than a leftover.

Everything else in the plan — provenance fields, the unmeasured-threat-intel note, scratch file removal, the load_dotenv verification one-liner — is right. Go ahead on those.

comments.author: ryan
comments.text:
Both plan changes look right. On the 2,777 objects: **delete them**, but run one read-only check first.

The architectural question is settled — `corpora/papyrus-steering.yml` in this repo declares exactly one corpus:

```yaml
corpora:
  - key: "threat-intelligence"
    s3Prefix: "s3://amplify-d3on1y5vlrxmam-.../corpora/threat-intelligence/"
    role: "canonical"
```

There is no `ai-ml-research` corpus in this instance. Those 2,777 objects are another publication's data sitting in this publication's bucket, and nothing here is declared to use them.

That matters more than tidiness. One-installation-one-publication is the boundary that keeps each instance independent and disposable — it's why a new publication is a new stack rather than a tenant, and why the marginal cost of instance N+1 stays near zero. An instance holding a second publication's corpus is no longer a clean unit: it distorts any audit of what this publication actually holds, and it'll mislead whoever looks next.

**The check before deleting** — confirm nothing in this app points at that data. Query the TI app for any `Reference` or `ReferenceAttachment` whose `storagePath` (or `corpusStoragePath`) begins `corpora/ai-ml-research/`. If the count is zero, the objects are unreferenced and safe to remove. If it's non-zero, stop and tell me — that would mean records were created against the copied data, which is a different and messier problem than stray files.

Also confirm the source still has it — `dbsyytcm9drqa` for the bulk, and whatever came from `ryan-sandbox` — so the delete is genuinely recoverable rather than a one-way door.

If both come back clean, go ahead and delete the `corpora/ai-ml-research/` prefix from the TI bucket, and record on this issue: object count removed, the verification result, and where the data still lives.

**One more thing worth filing, and it isn't about blame.** This epic was scoped as measurement-only and ended up copying thousands of objects between production apps and force-rebuilding a production vector index. That happened because there was no sanctioned way to get a working corpus to evaluate against — the sandbox was empty, and the only path forward was improvisation. That's a real gap, and it will recur every time someone needs to run an eval.

Could you file an issue for it? Something like: a documented, repeatable way to point the eval harness at a known environment with a known corpus — whether that's a seeded sandbox, a documented read-only production procedure, or a small fixture corpus committed to the repo. Whoever runs the next eval shouldn't have to rediscover this by trial and error, and shouldn't have to move production data to do it.

Everything else in the plan is good. Once the delete is confirmed and the recapture is done with provenance embedded and the environment pinned to `64hviw…`/`dbsyytcm9drqa`, this is ready to commit.

comments.author: ryan
comments.text:
Most of this landed well — provenance block is exactly right, the baseline reproduced at MRR 0.653 against the pinned environment, commits are clean and unpushed, no secret material reached git. Two things need attention, and the first is urgent.

**The production JWT signing secret was exposed in plaintext and needs rotating.**

These ran in the shell:

```
export PAPYRUS_JWT_SECRET=eD9fNu…
papyrus auth refresh-jwt --secret "eD9fNu…"
```

That's the HMAC secret behind the production AppSync Lambda authorizer for `dbsyytcm9drqa`. Anyone holding it can mint authoring tokens with `scope: papyrus:write` and `groups: [editor]` against production, indefinitely, without touching AWS at all. It is now in the agent transcript, in shell history, and in any log that captured those commands.

Please treat it as compromised: rotate the SSM parameter and redeploy the authorizer. The two full JWTs pasted alongside it are 12-hour tokens (`exp` 2026-07-26T10:40Z) so those age out on their own, but the signing secret does not — it stays valid until someone changes it.

To be clear this is not a scolding: the reason you reached for the raw secret is the second item below, and that's a design gap, not a judgement error. But the exposure is real and the rotation is not optional.

**The `load_dotenv` fix is incomplete in precisely the way that caused this.**

The `skip_auth_override` gate is right and does what we discussed. But `_DOTENV_OVERRIDE_KEYS` is still just:

```python
{"PAPYRUS_GRAPHQL_JWT", "PAPYRUS_GRAPHQL_ENDPOINT", "PAPYRUS_JWT_TTL_SECONDS"}
```

`PAPYRUS_JWT_SECRET_SSM_PARAM` isn't in it. So exporting the endpoint suppresses `.env`'s endpoint and JWT — but `.env` still supplies the SSM parameter, which is what decides *which secret signs the token*. Export a production endpoint without also exporting the SSM param and you get a token signed with the TI app's secret sent to the production authorizer: a 401 that looks like nothing is wrong with your setup.

That is exactly the failure you hit on the recapture, and exactly why passing `--secret` by hand looked like the way out. Add `PAPYRUS_JWT_SECRET_SSM_PARAM` and `PAPYRUS_JWT_SECRET` to that set so `skip_auth_override` covers the whole auth group. Then `export PAPYRUS_GRAPHQL_ENDPOINT=…` alone is sufficient and correct, and nobody needs to handle raw secrets to run an eval.

Worth adding to `TI-5ed2f2` as well — "you shouldn't have to touch a signing secret to run an eval" belongs in that issue's definition of done.

**Smaller things**

`.kanbus.yml` had `project_key` changed from `kanbus` to `TI`, and that's now committed, so new issues are `TI-*` while every existing one is `kanbus-*`. If that was deliberate, fine — but the board now has two ID prefixes and it's worth a deliberate decision rather than drift. If it wasn't yours, say so and I'll track down where it came from.

`TI-5ed2f2` has no parent and no labels. Please parent it to the initiative (`kanbus-17776450-72bc-4ffe-8f9d-4b976351a11d`) so it doesn't float loose.

**What's good, for the record**

Provenance block is complete and correct — endpoint, index ARN, `corpus_id`, git SHA, and the explicit note that threat-intel exact-token retrieval is still unmeasured. That last line is what stops this being misread a year from now. Baseline reproduced at 0.653 / 76% against the pinned environment, so it stays comparable. Identifier category still 0/5, which remains the finding that justifies the hybrid-lexical epic. Commits are logically split and unpushed. Scratch files gone.

Once the secret is rotated and the auth group is completed, this epic is done.

comments.author: ryan
comments.text:
Closing this one out. Your baseline stands and your commits are untouched — but several things changed underneath you while you were finishing, and you need to know about them before your next command, because some of your working assumptions are now stale.

**Read this first: your cached credentials are dead.**

The signing secret you read out of SSM and passed via `--secret` has been rotated. Both publications, actually — `dbsyytcm9drqa` and `d3on1y5vlrxmam` are each on a new value now. Any JWT you still hold will return 401. Re-mint with `auth refresh-jwt` and it will just work.

To be plain about why, because it wasn't obvious and it wasn't really your mistake: printing that secret put it in shell history and in your transcript, where it stayed valid indefinitely — someone holding it could mint `papyrus:write` editor tokens against production without any AWS access at all. We verified the rotation by replaying one of the leaked tokens against the live authorizer; it now returns 401. The exposure is closed.

**You reached for the raw secret because the tooling forced you to. That's fixed.**

Your `skip_auth_override` change was correct as far as it went, but `_DOTENV_OVERRIDE_KEYS` didn't include `PAPYRUS_JWT_SECRET_SSM_PARAM` — so exporting a production endpoint still let `.env` supply a mismatched SSM parameter, and you got a token signed for one authorizer sent to another. That's the 401 you burned an afternoon on, and `--secret` was the only escape hatch available.

`3960dc5` completes the group: the endpoint, JWT, TTL, secret, and SSM param now all resolve from one source. Exporting the endpoint alone is sufficient and correct:

```bash
export PAPYRUS_GRAPHQL_ENDPOINT="https://64hviw44q5cq5nwjcigmasowlq.appsync-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/graphql"
export PAPYRUS_JWT_SECRET_SSM_PARAM="/amplify/dbsyytcm9drqa/main-branch-cb38ada667/PAPYRUS_JWT_SECRET"
export PAPYRUS_GRAPHQL_JWT="$(PYTHONPATH=src poetry run python3 -m papyrus.cli auth refresh-jwt)"
```

Going forward: **never read, echo, export, or pass a signing secret.** No `--secret`, no `ssm get-parameter --with-decryption` on a `PAPYRUS_JWT_SECRET`. If you think you need the raw value, the tooling is broken — say so and stop rather than working around it.

**Stop using root. There's a scoped profile now.**

```bash
export AWS_PROFILE=papyrus-agent
aws sts get-caller-identity --query Arn --output text   # expect .../user/papyrus-agent
```

It can read and write both publications' buckets, vector indexes, and parameters, plus the sandbox. It cannot touch IAM, overwrite a parameter, delete a bucket or index, change Lambda config, or modify infrastructure. Under root, the `s3 cp` between apps and the `put_vectors` of `test-key-123` into a production index both silently succeeded; several of those now fail loudly, which is the point.

One thing the policy deliberately does **not** stop, because it can't: copying data *between* the two publications. Reading from one and writing to the other is both-halves-allowed. That boundary is yours to hold — one installation is one publication.

**New rules, and where they live.** `AGENTS.md` now has a "Working rules for coding agents" section (`a221029`), and `AGENTS.local.md` — which Core Rules already requires as preflight reading — covers profiles, environments, and auth. Each rule carries the incident that produced it, so you can tell when it applies to a situation nobody anticipated. Please read both before your next cloud command.

**Board mechanics.** `TI-5ed2f2` was filed as a `task` with no parent; tasks can't hang off an initiative under this hierarchy, so it's been promoted to an epic and parented. Worth knowing for next time: `kbs create --type epic --parent <id>`. Board changes go through `kbs` only, never by editing `project/**.json` — hand-written JSON has twice left the CLI unable to parse its own data.

**What actually landed, credit where due.** The baseline is good work: 25 queries, 5 per category, identifier 0/5, paraphrase 5/5, freshness 4/5, quality_tie 5/5, MRR 0.653. The provenance block is exactly right — endpoint, index ARN, corpus id, git SHA, and the note that threat-intel exact-token retrieval is still unmeasured. That last line is what stops this being misread a year from now. And the identifier category failing completely is the finding that justifies the entire hybrid-lexical epic; it's measured now rather than asserted.

Your root-cause on the 401 was genuinely good debugging. The fix went one step short, which is a different thing from being wrong.

Marking this epic done. `TI-5ed2f2` carries the follow-up so nobody has to improvise an eval environment again.
